There is a great book teaching the use of the "Memory Palace " system for chess …

THE CHESS MEMORY PALACE" by john Holden

Its self-published (I think)  
His contact is [...] Chess has become very memory specific since computer chess 'engines" now give you the best moves if you can remember them. creativity and genius … are less personal ( I sound bitter, but nay,) I am not invested enough to be so. it is what it is, Bobby Fisher was disgusted with this transformation of chess before he passed because he was invested and he was a genius, but not I, [...] I used to play highschool and a little bit of tournament chess when I was younger. I’m not a very good player myself, but a lot of my friends were quite good (not world class, but provincial or national level for South Africa).

For a decent (sighted) player being able to visualize the board and playing blindfolded is pretty normal, probably mostly a side effect of trying to work out move combinations and planning ahead several moves over and over.

Most of my friends could do this without specifically training for it or using any mnemonic techniques - it just sort of happened because they played so much and as part of playing they are visualizing future board configurations.

results.title: 🧠 Chess and Memory: Why Some Players Can Recall Thousands of Positions | Chesscul
results.content:
## The importance of long-term memory

Chess relies heavily on long-term memory. Every analyzed game becomes potential material for future decisions. Over time, the brain develops a massive internal database of useful experiences.

This memory is not static. It is constantly reorganized. Patterns are refined, corrected, and discarded when they are no longer valid.

Chess memory is dynamic, not archival.

## Why beginners forget everything

Beginners often become frustrated by how quickly they “forget” what they study: openings, tactics, endgames. This is not a failure of memory, but a lack of structure.

Without deep understanding, information does not stick. The brain cannot build stable patterns without knowing why things happen. [...] Weak pawns, open files, exposed kings, poorly coordinated pieces — these elements form a mental map. The brain does not store isolated data points, but relationships between them.

When that structure is absent, as in random positions, the memory advantage disappears.

## Remembering is not storing, it is recognizing

Chess memory does not function like a hard drive filled with thousands of images. Instead, it operates as a recognition system. The brain compares what it sees with past experience and immediately identifies similarities.

This process takes place in milliseconds and does not require conscious effort. That is why grandmasters can “remember” complex positions they have never encountered exactly before: they resemble thousands of others already internalized. [...] Memory without meaning is fragile. In chess, memorization without comprehension is almost useless.

## Studying versus training memory

Many players believe they are training their memory by mechanically memorizing opening lines. In reality, they are accumulating shallow information.

Expert memory is built through active analysis: questioning ideas, understanding plans, and examining the consequences of mistakes. The brain needs cognitive conflict to consolidate patterns.

Remembering thousands of positions is not about repetition — it is about deep understanding.

## Memory under pressure

Another striking feature of elite chess memory is its accessibility under extreme pressure. When time is short, the brain does not search slowly through stored information. It reacts.
